results.answer:
If you're a federal retiree with an OPM annuity and you aren't entitled to Social Security or RRB benefits, you must ask to have your Part B premiums deducted from your annuity. Contact your local Social Security office to make your request. Visit SSA.gov/locator to find your local office.

If your premiums aren't deducted from your OPM annuity, you'll get a bill for your Part B premium. Typically, Part B premiums are billed quarterly (every 3 months). If you also pay for Part A or Part D IRMAA, or use Medicare Easy Pay to pay your premiums, you'll get a monthly bill.

If you're billed, payment options include:
- Online: Visit Medicare.gov/account to log into (or create) your Medicare account. Then, select "Pay my premium" to make a payment by credit card, debit card, Health Savings Account (HSA) card, or from your checking or savings account. This free service is the fastest way to pay your premium.
- Medicare Easy Pay: This free service automatically deducts your payment (the excerpt cuts off here; the documents mention there are **4** ways to pay, but the others aren't included).

results.answer:
No deductible: Basic Option does not have a calendar year deductible. Instead, most services are subject to copayments ($35 for primary care providers and $50 for specialists).

Out-of-pocket maximum: For a Self Only enrollment, your out-of-pocket maximum for eligible coinsurance and copayment amounts is $7,500 when you use Preferred providers. When your eligible out-of-pocket expenses reach this catastrophic protection maximum, you no longer have to pay the associated cost-sharing amounts for the rest of the calendar year.

Things to keep in mind:
- Only eligible expenses for Preferred provider services count toward these limits.
- Some costs do not count toward this protection. These expenses do not count toward your catastrophic protection out-of-pocket maximum, and you must continue to pay them even after you reach it.
- Under Basic Option, you must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care.

So the most you'd pay in eligible cost-sharing in a year with PPO providers is **$7,500**, not counting excluded expenses.

On Basic Option, an MRI performed and billed by a hospital outpatient department falls under outpatient diagnostic testing and treatment services performed and billed by a facility, limited to: • Angiographies • Bone density tests • CT scans/MRIs/PET scans. Your cost depends on the facility type:

- Preferred facilities: **$250** copayment per day per facility
- Member facilities: **$250** copayment per day per facility
- Non-member facilities: **$250** copayment per day per facility, plus any difference between our allowance and the billed amount

- You pay 35% of the Plan allowance for agents or drugs administered or obtained in connection with your care. This could include contrast agents used during the MRI.
- You may be responsible for paying a higher copayment per day per facility if other diagnostic and/or treatment services are billed in addition to the services listed here.

results.answer:
Since your mom is on day 45, she falls in the days 21–100 range of her benefit period. Days 21–100: You pay $217 each day.

For context, the daily cost depends on how long she has been in the facility:
- Days 1–20: You pay $0 each day after you pay the $1,736 amount.
- Days 101 and beyond: You pay all costs.

The day count is tied to benefit periods. Your benefit period ends when you stop getting skilled nursing facility care for 60 days in a row. If you're admitted to the SNF again after those 60 days, a new benefit period will start.

If she is in a Medicare Advantage plan instead of Original Medicare, those plans can't charge more than Original Medicare for certain services, like chemotherapy, dialysis, and days 21–100 of skilled nursing facility care.

results.answer:
Completing the Blue Health Assessment (BHA) gets you a personalized health plan and the chance to earn health account dollars.

- **Health action plan:** Your BHA answers are evaluated to create a unique health action plan. Based on the results of your BHA, you can select personalized goals, receive supportive advice, and easily track your progress through our online coaching tool, Daily Habits.
- **Goal rewards:** We will add $40 to your health account for each goal achieved, up to a maximum of three goals per year.
- **Total possible:** By completing the BHA and a maximum of three health goals, you can earn up to a total of $170 in health account dollars. The excerpts don't state a separate amount for the BHA alone. Since three goals pay $120, that would leave **$50** for the BHA, but this is inferred rather than stated.
- **Qualifying goals:** Health account dollars are available only when you complete goals related to exercise, nutrition, weight management, stress, emotional health, heart disease, heart failure, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma.
- **Deadline:** You must complete the BHA and your selected goals during the calendar year in order to receive these incentives.

The BHA also matters for one other program. If you complete the Blue Health Assessment (BHA), and indicate that you have been diagnosed with hypertension, and at least one medical claim has been processed during the past 12 months with a reported diagnosis of hypertension, you can qualify for a free blood pressure monitor. You are eligible to receive a free BPM every two calendar years.

These features apply to both Standard and Basic Option.

results.answer:
Under the Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan, you place your first mail order through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program, run by CVS Caremark. The steps are:

- Complete the initial mail order form;
- Enclose your prescription and copayment;
- Mail your order to CVS Caremark, P.O. Box 1590, Pittsburgh, PA 15230-1590

You should allow up to two weeks for delivery. Later orders are quicker: allow up to ten days for delivery on refills.

You can also skip mailing the form. Your physician may call in your initial prescription at 800-262-7890, TTY: 711. In that case you are responsible for the copayment.

Eligibility depends on your option:

- **Standard Option:** Standard Option members may use our Mail Service Prescription Drug Program to fill their prescriptions.
- **Basic Option:** The Mail Service Prescription Drug Program is available only to members with primary Medicare Part B coverage under Basic Option.

If your drug needs prior approval, the program won't fill it until you have that approval. CVS Caremark, the program administrator, will hold your prescription for you up to 30 days. If prior approval is not obtained within 30 days, your prescription will be unable to be filled. Also, specialty drugs will not be dispensed through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program.

results.question: If a doctor doesn't accept assignment, what's the most extra they can charge me above the Medicare-approved amount?

results.answer:
In many cases, a doctor who doesn't accept assignment can charge you no more than **15%** above the Medicare-approved amount. They can charge you more than the Medicare-approved amount. In many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge."

The FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield brochure says the same thing as a percentage of the base amount: a physician who does not accept Medicare assignment may not bill you for more than 115% of the amount Medicare bases its payment on, called the "limiting charge." If your physician tries to collect more than allowed by law, ask the physician to reduce the charges. If the physician does not, report the physician to the Medicare carrier that sent you the MSN form.

Also, you might have to pay the entire charge at the time of service.

results.question: How do I appeal a decision about a claim under Original Medicare?

results.answer:
If you have Original Medicare, the appeal starts with your **Medicare Summary Notice (MSN)**:

- Get the "Medicare Summary Notice" (MSN) that shows the item or service you're appealing.
- Circle the item(s) on the MSN you disagree with. Write an explanation of why you disagree with the decision. You can write on the MSN or on a separate piece of paper and attach it to the MSN.
- Include your name, phone number, and Medicare Number on the MSN. Keep a copy for your records.
- Send the MSN, or a copy, to the company that handles bills for Medicare (Medicare Administrative Contractor) listed on the MSN. You can include any information you have about your appeal, like information from your health care provider.

Instead of the MSN, you can use Form CMS-20027. To get this form, visit Medicare.gov/basics/forms-publications-mailings/forms/appeals, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to have a copy mailed to you. TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

Deadlines and decisions:
- You must file your appeal by the date in the MSN. If you missed the deadline for appealing, you may still file an appeal and get a decision if you can show good cause for missing the deadline.
- You'll generally get a decision from the Medicare Administrative Contractor within **60 days** after they get your request. If Medicare will cover the item(s) or service(s), it will be listed on your next MSN.

You can ask your doctor, supplier, or other health care provider for any information to make your appeal stronger, and you should keep a copy of everything related to your appeal. You can also get help filing an appeal from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

results.answer:
The yearly Part B deductible is **$283 in 2026**. Under Original Medicare, if the Part B deductible applies, you must pay all costs (up to the Medicare-approved amount) until you meet the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).

I can't reliably tell you which Medigap plans pay it. The comparison chart has a "Medicare Part B deductible" row, but the extracted text is garbled: Medicare Part B deductible 100% | 100% | 100%** 100%**. It shows four entries without the plan letters (A, B, C, D, F, G, K, L, M, N) they belong to. If a box is empty, it means that service isn't covered by that Medigap plan and you're responsible for paying the cost.

Related details from the same page:
- Plans K and L pay 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year after you meet your out-of-pocket yearly limit and your yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).
- You can't buy Medigap Plans C or F if you became eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020
- For the high-deductible versions of Plans F and G, you must pay up to $2,950 in 2026 for Medicare-covered costs (coinsurance, copayments, and deductibles) before your policy starts to pay.

To see which plans cover the Part B deductible, check the original chart on page 80 of Medicare & You.

results.answer:
Generally no. Under Basic Option you must use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits. There are no benefits for care performed by Participating and Non-participating providers.

There are some exceptions:
- **Emergency care:** You must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care. For the full list, see Section 3 for exceptions under What you must do to get covered care.
- **Overseas care:** The Basic Option requirement to use Preferred providers in order to receive benefits does not apply when you receive overseas care.
- **Medicare:** If you also have Medicare, the same rule applies. Under Basic Option, you must see Preferred providers in order to receive benefits.
